title: 魔鬼氈的發明（The Invention of Velcro）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 113 年學測閱讀測驗〈魔鬼氈的發明〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: One morning in 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral went for a walk in the woods with his dog. Back home, he found burrs, the sticky seed cases of some plants, stuck to the dog’s fur and his pants. Under a microscope, he saw that the burrs had many tiny hooks that clung firmly to the loops in the fabric. Seeing how tightly the hooks and loops held together, he {11} that if he could copy this design, he could produce a strong fastener—something that holds two things together—with many uses. Finding the right fabric for a strong bond was his first challenge. Cotton proved too soft, so after years of testing, he chose nylon, a strong man-made material. By 1955, he {12} a version that stayed closed yet was easy to pull apart when needed. That year, the product, named “Velcro,” received a Swiss patent, and de Mestral opened factories in Europe and, eventually, North America to {13} it on a large scale. At first, though, Velcro was not a success. Most fashion critics considered it ugly and cheap-looking. {14} , its use was limited to athletic equipment. In the early 1960s, however, the fastener finally {15} when NASA began using it in items sent into space with astronauts. Today, de Mestral’s design is found almost everywhere, from clothing and shoes to toys and airline seats.

title: 摩根奇幻樂園（Morgan’s Wonderland）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 110 年學測閱讀測驗〈摩根奇幻樂園〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Morgan’s Wonderland, located in San Antonio, Texas, is a theme park intended mainly for children with mental or physical disabilities. The park was built by Gordon Hartman, a former real estate developer, and was inspired by his daughter, Morgan, who has physical challenges and severe cognitive delays, or slow mental development. Morgan’s Wonderland opened in the spring of 2010 as the world’s first ultra-accessible family fun park—that is, a park that people with any disability can easily use. Admission is free for guests with special needs, and tickets for the general public are heavily discounted {11} people of all ages and abilities can come together and play in a safe environment. Completely wheelchair-accessible, the park offers 25 acres of {12} , including rides, playgrounds, a catch-and-release fishing lake, and picnic areas throughout the grounds. The rides have all been {13} for wheelchair users, so every member of the family can join in the fun. In June 2017, the park celebrated the opening of Morgan’s Inspiration Island. This {14} is made up of five themed splash pads—play areas where water sprays up from the ground—and a riverboat ride. There, guests in wheelchairs can {15} special waterproof chairs and enjoy the water without risking damage to their own wheelchairs. “Morgan taught me that there’s more to life in many ways than what I saw before,” said Hartman.

title: 巴西戰舞卡波耶拉（Capoeira）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 106 年學測閱讀測驗〈巴西戰舞卡波耶拉〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Capoeira is a martial art—a style of fighting—that also includes acrobatics, drumming, singing, and dance. {11} its dancelike appearance, it shares many basic techniques with other martial arts. Capoeira was created nearly 500 years ago in Brazil by African slaves. {12} from their homes against their will, they first developed it as a means of self-defense. But before long, Capoeira was no longer only for protection; it also became a powerful weapon in their life-or-death struggle against the slave owners. When the owners realized the power of Capoeira, they began to punish anyone who practiced it. The slaves therefore learned to {13} the forbidden fights with singing, clapping, and dancing, as though Capoeira were simply entertainment. The slave owners were not the only ones against Capoeira. At first, the Brazilian government also {14} it. However, a man known as Mestre Bimba devoted a great deal of time and effort to convincing the government that it had great cultural value and should become an official fighting style. He succeeded and turned the martial art into Brazil’s national sport. Bimba was also among the first to open Capoeira schools, which helped the art {15} around the world. Nowadays, Capoeira can be seen in movies and music videos, and it is believed to have influenced breaking and other hip-hop dance styles.

African slaves in Brazil created it nearly 500 years ago for self-defense. When their owners punished them for it, they hid the fighting behind music and dancing.
The Brazilian government first made the art illegal, but Mestre Bimba persuaded officials of its cultural worth, and it became the national sport.
Bimba’s early schools spread the art worldwide. Today it appears in films and music videos and is thought to have shaped breaking and other hip-hop dances.

title: 泰武國小古謠傳唱隊（Taiwu Elementary School Folk Singers）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 104 年學測閱讀測驗〈泰武國小古謠傳唱隊〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: In 2009, the Taiwu Elementary School Folk Singers were invited to perform in Europe. Camake Valaule, a physical education teacher and the group’s founder, admitted he was very nervous on their first European tour. Since most of the 75-minute show was a cappella, that is, sung without instruments, he feared the audience would fall asleep. {11} , the listeners paid close attention from start to finish. They later told him that through the songs, they had formed a {12} of the singers’ village without having to visit it. According to Camake, singing traditional ballads, or folk songs, has also helped the students and their parents {13} their own culture. It used to be that only tribal elders aged between 50 and 60 could sing these songs. Hearing their children perform them, many parents have begun to wonder why they themselves cannot sing these ballads. Now, it is often the children {14} the songs to their parents. Although the group has become famous abroad, fame was never Camake’s goal when he founded it in 2006. What mattered most was helping the children understand why they sing these songs and helping them preserve their culture. After Typhoon Morakot struck in August 2009, the school and the village had to {15} to a new site. “We could not take the forest or our houses with us,” Camake said, “but we could bring our culture along.”

title: 紅杉的生態（The Ecology of Redwood Trees）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 100 年學測閱讀測驗〈紅杉的生態〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Redwood trees are the tallest plants on Earth, reaching heights of up to 100 meters. They are also known for their {11} , typically 500 to 1,000 years but sometimes more than 2,000 years. The trunk of a redwood is huge and usually forms a single straight column. It is covered with a soft, spongy bark, which can be well over two feet thick in mature trees. This bark gives older trees some protection from insects, but its main {12} is that it keeps the center of the tree intact, or undamaged, during moderate forest fires. This resistance to fire explains why the giant redwood can live so long. While most other trees are destroyed by forest fires, the redwood actually prospers {13} them. Moderate fires clear the ground of competing plants, and the rising heat dries and opens the ripe cones of the redwood, releasing thousands of seeds onto the soil below. Besides seeds, new trees often grow from sprouts, young trees that form at the base of the trunk. These sprouts grow slowly and {14} the root system of the “mother” tree for food. When the main tree dies, the sprouts are free to grow as full trees, forming a “fairy ring,” or circle of trees, around the original tree. These trees, {15} , may give rise to more sprouts, and the cycle continues.
zh: 紅杉是地球上最高的植物，可以長到 100 公尺高。紅杉也以長壽聞名，通常能活 500 到 1,000 年，有時甚至超過 2,000 年。紅杉的樹幹非常粗大，通常長成一根筆直的柱子，外面覆蓋著一層柔軟、像海綿一樣的樹皮；比較成熟的樹，樹皮厚度可以超過兩英尺。這層樹皮讓老樹在某種程度上不受昆蟲侵害，但它最主要的好處是，遇到中等規模的森林火災時，能保護樹心完好無損。這種耐火的能力，就是巨大的紅杉能活那麼久的原因。大部分其他的樹木會毀於森林火災，紅杉卻反而因為森林火災長得更好。中等規模的火災會清除地面上和紅杉競爭的植物，上升的熱氣也會烘乾成熟的紅杉毬果，讓毬果張開，把成千上萬顆種子撒在下方的土地上。除了種子之外，新的樹也常常從嫩芽長出來，嫩芽就是在樹幹基部長出的小樹苗。這些嫩芽長得很慢，靠「母樹」的根系取得養分。母樹死了以後，嫩芽就能自由長成大樹，在原來那棵樹的周圍形成一圈「仙女環」，也就是環狀的樹群。這些樹接著又可能長出更多嫩芽，就這樣循環下去。

These trees, {15} , may give rise to more sprouts, ~~and~~ the cycle continues.
outline: Redwoods are the tallest plants on the planet, rising as high as 100 meters, and many of them survive for centuries, some for over two thousand years.
Their huge trunks are wrapped in soft bark more than two feet thick, which guards the core during moderate fires and lets the trees reach great ages.
Fires that kill most other trees help redwoods grow: they burn away rival plants, and their heat opens ripe cones so that thousands of seeds drop.
Sprouts at the base of the trunk draw food from the mother tree’s roots. When she dies, they grow into a ring of trees that produce sprouts of their own.

title: 紐西蘭特有種昆蟲威塔（The Weta, a Native Insect of New Zealand）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 99 年學測閱讀測驗〈紐西蘭特有種昆蟲威塔〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: In New Zealand, there is a grasshopper-like insect that is found nowhere else on earth. New Zealanders have given it the nickname weta, which in Maori—the language of the country’s native people—means “god of bad looks.” Most people feel disgusted {11} these bulky, slow-moving bugs. Wetas are nocturnal—they come out of their caves and holes only after dark. A giant weta can grow to over three inches long and weigh as much as 1.5 ounces. Just like their cousins the grasshoppers and crickets, wetas are able to “sing” by {12} parts of their legs together or against their lower bodies. Not many people are likely to feel sympathy for these endangered creatures. {13} , they do need protecting. The slow and clumsy wetas have been around in New Zealand since the age of the dinosaurs. There they evolved and survived in an environment where they had no {14} until rats arrived with European immigrants. Rats, which love to hunt and eat wetas, have become a real problem for many native species that are not used to their presence, and they {15} a serious threat to the native weta population.

title: 高爾夫球的演進（The Evolution of the Golf Ball）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 110 年指考閱讀測驗〈高爾夫球的演進與凹洞的空氣動力學原理〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Since golf began in the 15th century, the game has seen many advances, including significant changes to the golf ball. Early golfers played with a wooden ball until it {11} the Featherie, a leather bag stuffed with feathers. In 1848 came the Gutta Percha ball, which was far more durable and affordable. The next {12} came in the early 1900s with the Haskell, the first ball with a rubber core, which could travel up to 20 yards farther than the Gutta Percha ball. In 1905, William Taylor introduced the first ball covered with dimples, or tiny cup-shaped marks. By the 1930s, golf balls with rows of dimples were accepted as the standard design. These tiny marks play an important role in a golf ball’s {13} because they improve its aerodynamics, or the way it moves through the air. In flight, a ball experiences two major forces: lift and drag. Dimples reduce drag, the force that pulls back on the ball, so it can travel faster and farther. They also force the airflow downward, which pushes the ball upward. Airplanes depend on the same {14} to stay in the air. In general, balls with small, shallow dimples tend to have a longer, lower flight path, whereas those with deeper dimples fly higher. {15} , golfers can choose their balls based on what they need for a particular shot or for particular weather.

text: Demolition is the tearing-down of buildings and other structures. You can easily {11} a five-story building with heavy machines such as excavators and wrecking balls, but for a 20-story skyscraper, explosive demolition is the preferred method. To demolish a building safely, blasters, or explosives experts, must map out a careful plan ahead of time. The first step is to study the building’s blueprints to understand how it is put together. Next, the crew tours the building, noting the support structure of each floor. With the data in hand, the blasters {12} a plan of attack, deciding what explosives to use, where to place them, and how to time each explosion. Blasters usually set off explosives on the support columns of the lower floors first and then on a few upper floors. In most cases, blowing up the lower floors is enough to collapse the building. {13} , loading explosives on upper floors helps break the building material apart as it falls. Smaller pieces {14} an easier cleanup after the blast. The hardest part of bringing a building down is {15} the direction in which it falls, so that it comes down where the crew wants it to. title: 馬里亞納海溝的深海汙染（Deep-Sea Pollution in the Mariana Trench）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 109 年指考閱讀測驗〈馬里亞納海溝的深海汙染〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: The planet’s deepest point lies in the Mariana Trench—a long, narrow valley on the floor of the Pacific Ocean. According to a new study, even in this remote place, sea creatures cannot escape pollution. A team of researchers recently sent a remotely operated vehicle into the depths of the trench. In the small hard-shelled animals it brought back, the researchers found extremely high levels of prohibited industrial chemicals. These animals were heavily {11} , with levels of toxins, or poisons, 50 times higher than those found in the most heavily polluted rivers in the world. {12} , all the chemicals found were “persistent organic pollutants” (POPs), meaning they stay in the environment for a very long time. PCBs, one of the most common types, were once widely used in industry, but they {13} in the United States in the 1970s after being linked to cancer. These compounds stick to the surface of materials like plastic. Many sea creatures mistakenly eat this colorful but toxic material, so the chemicals build up inside them. When these animals die, their {14} sink to the ocean floor, where deep-sea creatures feed on them. This is how the pollutants pass from one creature to another along the food chain. The fact that the trench lies many miles away from any industrial source suggests that these pollutants can travel {15} , despite having been prohibited worldwide decades ago.

These compounds stick to the surface of materials like plastic. The chemicals belong to a group that lasts for decades in nature. PCBs, a common type, were outlawed in the US in the 1970s over cancer fears.

Because the trench lies far from any factory, the pollutants seem to have journeyed a great way, though the world stopped using them decades ago.

text: In March 2022, the Endurance—the lost ship of the polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—was found in Antarctica, 107 years after it sank. The news made headlines around the world partly because the discovery {11} the final chapter in a legendary story of courage. In August 1914, Shackleton and a crew of 27 set sail on the Endurance, hoping to make the first land crossing of Antarctica. After leaving South Georgia Island in December, the ship ran into floating ice and was soon completely {12} in pack ice, or huge sheets of sea ice pressed tightly together. For nine months, the sturdy ship {13} , drifting slowly south and then being pushed north by the ice. Gradually, the pressure of the ice bent its wooden boards, and freezing water rushed in. On October 27, 1915, Shackleton ordered his men to abandon the ship, which sank a few weeks later. By the time the men sailed in lifeboats to Elephant Island, where no one lived, they {14} five months camping on the drifting ice. They could not survive there for long, so Shackleton and five others sailed 800 miles across stormy seas to South Georgia Island for help. Help was almost at hand, but ice and bad weather kept them from returning to the island. {15} , Shackleton returned to Elephant Island on August 30, 1916, with a ship to rescue the rest of his men. Every member of the team survived, but the Endurance stayed lost until 2022.

title: 馬賽人的文化與傳統（The Culture and Traditions of the Maasai People）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 111 年學測閱讀測驗〈馬賽人的文化與傳統〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Standing proud on the savannah, or open grassland, with their red blankets and painted shields, the Maasai are a widely known symbol of East Africa. The Maasai of Kenya and northern Tanzania are semi-nomadic: they wander from place to place with their herds and live almost entirely on the animals’ meat, blood, and milk. Over the years, these {11} people have stood strong against slavery and resisted their governments’ urging to adopt a more modern lifestyle. {12} , they are one of the few tribes that have kept most of their traditions. Until recently, a Maasai boy could become a warrior only by killing a lion on his own. Maasai clothing {13} age, gender, and place. Red is a popular color, and women generally opt for checked, striped, or patterned cloth. Young men wear black for several months after a ceremony that marks their coming of age. Beadwork—jewelry made of tiny colored balls called beads—is also an important part of Maasai culture. Made by women, it is famous for its complexity. Before trade with Europeans began in the 19th century, beads were made of natural materials such as clay, shells, and ivory. Those materials were later replaced by colorful glass beads, {14} made more detailed designs and color patterns possible. Multicolored beadwork is popular among both men and women. Each color {15} a special meaning: white stands for peace, green for land and production, and red—the Maasai’s favorite color—for unity and bravery.

title: 白宮的歷史（The History of the White House）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 107 年學測閱讀測驗〈白宮的歷史〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: For more than two hundred years, the White House has stood as a symbol of the American presidency and the American people. As plans for a new capital began in 1790, a {11} was held to find a builder for the “President’s House.” Nine designs were submitted, and James Hoban, an Irish-born architect, won the gold medal for his practical and handsome design. Although George Washington oversaw the construction, he never lived in the house. In 1800, President John Adams and his wife became its first residents. American presidents can express their own style in how they decorate the house and how they receive the public. Thomas Jefferson held the first inaugural open house in 1805—after he was sworn in, many who had watched him take the oath simply followed him home. Jefferson also opened the house for public tours, a {12} that has continued ever since, except during wartime. In addition, he held receptions on New Year’s Day and the Fourth of July. Abraham Lincoln later {13} these customs, but the inaugural crowds grew far too large for the house to hold, creating a security problem. Effective crowd control measures to {14} the problem were not introduced until Grover Cleveland’s first term. At various times, the White House went by several other names, such as the “President’s Palace” and the “Executive Mansion.” {15} , President Theodore Roosevelt officially gave the building its present name in 1901.

Each dog is placed in one of nine groups. Besides being fun to share, the results explain dog behavior and bring pets and owners closer.

title: 自動駕駛汽車的未來（The Future of Driverless Cars）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 103 年學測閱讀測驗〈自動駕駛汽車的未來〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Today the car seems to take a big leap forward every few years. Many new cars now {11} driver assistance technologies that let them park themselves, read traffic signs, and brake to avoid crashes. Carmakers are also testing Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication, or V2V. V2V uses wireless signals to send each car’s location, speed, and direction back and forth between cars, so that they keep safe distances from each other. Another system being tested, Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communication, or V2I, would link cars with nearby road signs, traffic lights, and traffic management systems. Through V2I, cars could {12} drivers to safety problems ahead and help them find the best routes. Both V2V and V2I could prevent around 80 percent of crashes. {13} , a number of firms are going a step further, building cars that drive themselves to a chosen destination without a human at the controls. Google already uses prototypes, or test versions, of such cars to carry its staff along California freeways. It once filmed one of them {14} a blind man to a fast-food restaurant for takeout hamburgers. If and when cars go completely driverless, the benefits will be enormous. Huge numbers of elderly and disabled people could regain their mobility—the freedom to get around on their own. The young will not have to pay costly car insurance, because their {15} hands and feet will no longer touch the wheel or the gas pedal. Commuters will gain hours each day to rest, read, or work.

title: 現代廢水的淨化流程（How Wastewater Is Cleaned Today）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 109 年指考閱讀測驗〈現代廢水處理流程〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Early civilizations often built drainage systems in cities to carry away rainwater that ran down the streets during storms. As cities grew more crowded, however, these old systems could no longer {11} the rising amount of water flowing into them. During the Industrial Revolution, waste from factories was also added to sewage—the dirty water from homes—so better ways of handling it were needed even more. In the mid-19th century, the first steps were taken to clean wastewater. Modern wastewater {12} is the process of removing harmful physical, chemical, and biological elements from sewage. It starts with screening out large objects such as paper and wood, as well as heavy materials like dirt. The water then passes into a series of concrete tanks. In the primary tanks, human waste, called sludge, settles to the bottom, while oils and grease float to the top, where they are collected. {13} , organic matter such as eggshells and coffee grounds is broken down into smaller substances. Next, the sewage moves into the secondary tanks, where the solids that were not removed earlier {14} through decomposition, a process that digests the material. After that, the liquid is filtered through sand, which gets rid of almost all bacteria and tiny solid particles. Finally, the chemical chlorine is added in the last tanks to {15} the remaining bacteria. Once the bacteria are destroyed, the chlorine is taken out, and the clean water is released into a river or the ocean.

In the first tanks, sludge sinks while oils rise and get collected; later, decomposition and sand filters take out most solids and bacteria.
In the last stage, chlorine destroys the bacteria left in the water; the chlorine is then taken out, and the clean water flows into rivers or the sea.

title: 妮娜號複製船上的動手學習（Hands-on Learning aboard the Nina Replica Ship）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 105 年指考閱讀測驗〈妮娜號複製船上的動手學習〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Some people call the Nina a traveling museum, while others refer to it as a living or open-air museum. Built in Brazil {11} the 500th anniversary of Columbus’ first voyage to the New World, the Nina is a replica—an exact copy—of Columbus’ favorite ship, showing visitors how large the original was and what sailing tools were used more than 500 years ago. I joined the crew of the Nina in February 2013. My goal was to {12} my days aboard the ship in a blog as part of a research project sponsored by my university. {13} , I gained my most valuable insights when I watched or guided school-age children on tours of the ship. The field-trip tour of the Nina is hands-on learning, or learning by doing, at its best. On board, students could touch the ropes, pass around a ballast stone—a heavy rock that helps keep a ship steady—and move the extremely large tiller that steered ships in Columbus’ day. They soon came to {14} the hard work involved in sailing a ship back in his time. I was pleased to see the students become active participants in their own learning. My experience on the Nina {15} my long-held belief that students stay interested, ask better questions, and think more deeply when they are actively engaged in learning. The students who boarded the Nina came as passive learners. They left as bold explorers.

title: 土耳其哥樂美國家公園：自然與人文（Goreme National Park: Where Nature Meets Man）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 104 年指考閱讀測驗〈土耳其哥樂美國家公園：自然與人文〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: With soaring rock formations and mysterious underground cities, Goreme National Park is an incredible tourist attraction in central Turkey. Thousands of years ago, ancient volcanoes poured out layer upon layer of thick ash and lava, which formed the Cappadocia region, where the park now stands. Over the centuries, wind and rain {11} this land, carving out valleys and leaving behind towering rock pillars as tall as 40 meters. These pillars are known as “fairy chimneys.” They {12} an extraordinary range of shapes and sizes, but most are tall and look like giant mushrooms with a cap on top. The cap is the hardest part of each pillar and protects the softer rock below from the weather. The cap, however, does not last forever. {13} , it falls off, and wind and rain cut away the rest of the pillar until it, too, collapses. But Goreme is more than its dramatic scenery. Humans, too, have left their mark on the region. In the fourth century, the Byzantine Christians inhabited, or lived in, the area. They carved thousands of cave churches out of rock. Many of them were decorated with beautiful wall paintings whose colors still {14} all their original freshness. These Christians even dug out entire underground villages to hide from the Romans and, later, the Muslims. To this day, many of these villages are still inhabited, and families {15} grapes, potatoes, and flat bread in rock-cut storerooms for the winter.

title: 松露的特性、採集與保存（Characteristics, Harvesting, and Preservation of Truffles）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 100 年指考閱讀測驗〈松露的特性、採集與保存〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Since the days of the ancient Greeks and Romans, truffles have been used in Europe as delicacies, or fine foods, and even as medicines. Today they are among the most expensive natural foods in the world, often {11} as much as US$250 to US$450 per pound. Truffles are actually mushrooms, but unusual ones. They live in close association with the roots of certain trees and grow underground. This is why they are difficult to find. In Europe, truffles are harvested with the help of female pigs or trained dogs. Female pigs are especially sensitive to the odor of truffles because it is similar to the smell {12} by male pigs. The use of pigs is risky, though, because they tend to eat anything remotely edible, or fit to eat. For this reason, dogs have been trained to dig into the ground wherever they {13} this odor, and they willingly exchange their truffle for a piece of bread and a pat on the head. To enjoy the wonderful flavor of what has been described as a jewel of the earth, you must eat truffles fresh and uncooked, shortly after they are dug up. Female pigs and trained dogs sniff out truffles in Europe. Since pigs eat almost anything, hunters train dogs, which happily trade their finds for bread.

title: 美國對狼的戰爭（The War on Wolves in America）
flagNote: 本題庫改編練習：文章改編自 95 年指考閱讀測驗〈美國對狼的戰爭〉，刪短後照現行學測綜合測驗的版面出題（第 11–15 題，每題四選一），參考答案與解析由本題庫撰寫，沒有官方答對率。
text: Native Americans could not understand the white man’s war on the wolf. The Lakota, Blackfeet, and Shoshone, among other tribes, considered the wolf their spiritual brother. They respected its endurance, or its ability to keep going for a long time, and its skill at hunting. Warriors wrapped themselves in wolf skins, hoping to {11} the wolf’s courage and endurance. The best Comanche warriors were even called wolves. White settlers, {12} , saw the wolf as an enemy to be destroyed. Western ranchers, who raised cattle, complained that wolves killed thousands of their animals each year. In 1884, Montana created its first wolf bounty—a cash reward for every dead wolf. Over thirty-five years, hunters brought in more than eighty thousand dead wolves to {13} the reward, and the government even provided free poison. Finally, in 1914, ranchers persuaded Congress to provide money to kill wolves on public lands. No place was safe for the last wolves in the American West, not even Yellowstone, the nation’s first national park. From the day the park opened in 1872, poisoned meat was {14} to kill wolves. In October 1926, two young wolves trapped near a dead bison became the last animals killed in the park’s wolf control program. Ranchers had won the war against the wolf. Only in the northern woods of Wisconsin, Minnesota, and Michigan could the howl of gray wolves still be heard, while the vast lands of the American West {15} . The country had lost its greatest predator.

outline: Several Native American tribes treated the wolf as a spiritual brother, admired its endurance and hunting skill, and wore wolf skins to gain its qualities.
White settlers took the opposite view. Ranchers blamed wolves for cattle losses, Montana paid for dead wolves, and the government supplied poison and federal money.
Even Yellowstone offered no protection. Poison was used against wolves from the park’s earliest days, and the last animals its control program killed were two young wolves in 1926.
With the ranchers victorious, wild gray wolves survived only in a few northern forests, leaving the West quiet and without its top hunter.
